     INTERVENOR THE WALKER FAMILY’S INITIAL POST-HEARING BRIEF

       Intervenors Sam Walker, John Walker, Jennifer Walker, and Lucy Walker (the “Walker

Family”) file their Initial Post-Hearing Brief and request that the Administrative Law Judges

(“ALJs”) issue a proposal for decision recommending that the Public Utility Commission of Texas

(the “PUC” or “Commission”) approve Applicants Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC

(“Oncor”) and LCRA Transmission Service Corporation (“LCRA”)’s (collectively “Applicants”)

recommended Route 894. In support of the requested relief, the Walker Family respectfully offers

the following:

                 I.    INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT

       Applicants seek approval from the Commission for the construction of a 765-kV

transmission line from Bell County south of Temple, Texas, to Big Hill, Texas, south of San

Angelo (the “Application” or the “Project”). Over the course of the five-day hearing on the merits,

Route 894, the Applicants’ best meets route, proved to be just that, the best possible route that

should be approved by the Commission.




                                                3
        The evidence will show that Route 894 best satisfies Public Utility Regulatory Act’s

(“PURA’s”) statutory factors on prudent avoidance, environmental integrity, paralleling, and

community values. None of the parties, including Commission Staff, put forth convincing

arguments for the Commission to disagree with the Applicants. In fact, Commission Staff would

have the Commission diverge from the best meets route, and select Route 487, despite admitting

his recommendation was made without reviewing the parties’ testimonies. Any recommendation

with as significant of a record omission as this one cannot be relied upon by the Commission.

       Also critical, the Walker Family property on Link J11 contains a large drainage facility,

the only flood retardant structure posed to be impacted by any route. As the record shows, the

Walker Family has reasonable environmental and safety concerns regarding the impacts of a

765-kV line crossing one of these structures. The record also shows that neither the Applicants nor

Commission Staff considered these impacts when selecting a line. Given the uncertainty of these

impacts, the prudent choice would be to avoid the drainage facilities all together. Selecting

Applicants Route 894 would do so.

       For the reasons explained below, the Walker Family respectfully requests that the ALJs

issue a Proposal for Decision selecting Route 894.

                                  II.     ISSUES TO BE ADDRESSED

       The Commission identified twenty-one issues and sub-issues to be addressed in this

proceeding.1 However, because certain issues fall solely within the Applicants’ burden of proof,

were not contested by the intervenors, or are otherwise not relevant to the Walker Family’s

property’s location, the Walker Family submits briefing only on the following issues: Route,

Prudent Avoidance Policy, Paralleling, Costs, Consensus for Route 894, Failures of Route 487,


       1
           Order of Referral and Preliminary Order, March 30, 2026.

 Environmental Integrity, Community Values including Proximity to State Parks, Fragmentation,

Commission Staff’s Incomplete Review, Flood Control and Flooding Structures, and Proximity to

                                         III.   ARGUMENT

A.     Legal Standard

       An application for a certificate of convenience and necessity for a transmission line must

comply with the PURA. Specifically, Section 37.056 for “grant or denial of certificate” outlines

factors the Commission shall consider prior to approving an application. The Commission must

consider adequacy of existing service, community values, recreational and park areas, historical

and aesthetic values, and environmental integrity.2

       16 Texas Administrative Code (“TAC”) § 25.101(b)(3)(B) requires that an application for

a new transmission line address the criteria set forth in PURA § 37.056(c) and, considering those

criteria, engineering constraints, and costs, the line must be routed to the extent reasonable to

moderate the impact on the affected community and landowners. Oncor and LCRA TSC’s

recommended Route 894 best meets the necessary criteria established by the Legislature for

approval of an application to amend Certificate of Convenience and Necessity (“CCN”) while also

mitigating impacts to affected landowners. The criteria includes:

       (i)       whether the routes parallel or utilize existing compatible rights-of-way for
                 electric facilities, including the use of vacant positions on existing multiple
                 circuit transmission lines;

       (ii)      whether the routes parallel or utilize other existing compatible rights-of-
                 way, including roads, highways, railroads, or telephone utility rights-of-
                 way;

       (iii)     whether the routes parallel property lines or other natural or cultural
                 features; and


       2
           PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(A)-(E).



                                                   5
         (iv)       whether the routes conform with the policy of prudent avoidance.3

        The policy of prudent avoidance is a Commission routing principle intended to minimize

the exposure of the public to electric and magnetic fields (“EMF”) and to avoid, where reasonable,

placing transmission facilities in close proximity to habitable structures and areas of concentrated

human activity.4 Routing moderation to avoid sensitive environmental features, whose degradation

could impact human activity, when there is little to no EMF exposure to the public is consistent

with the policy of prudent avoidance.

B.      Route 894 best meets PURA’s statutory criteria and the Commission’s rules.

        1.         Route 894—rather than Route 487—best satisfies the policy of prudent
                   avoidance.

        Route 894, Applicants’ Preferred Route, outperforms Route 487, Staff’s Route, on the

Commission’s policy of prudent avoidance, the routing principle intended to limit exposures to

electric and magnetic fields (“EMF”) that can be avoided with reasonable investments of money

and effort.5 Prudent avoidance is achieved by minimizing the number of habitable structures

located in close proximity to the routes.6 With only 85 habitable structures within 500 feet of its

centerline, Route 894 outperforms the 96 habitable structures found within the same proximity to

Route 487.7 Wulff Bluff Creek Ranch’s witness, Dr. Turnbough, who has experience testifying in

over thirty PUC electric line cases, agrees that preventing negative impacts to habitable structures

 should be a high priority in this case.8 With a low number of habitable structures within 500 feet

of its centerline, Route 894 most satisfies the Commission’s policy of prudent avoidance.

       At the hearing, a few parties attempted to downplay the direct relationship between

habitable structures and prudent avoidance. However, Applicants’ witness, Brenda Perkins,

explained that the number of habitable structures affected is directly tied to prudent avoidance.9

The Application seeks to transmit substantially more energy than any other transmission line

installed to date in Texas. Perkins acknowledges that the real-life impacts of 765-kV lines on

habitable structures remains unknown, highlighting the preference for routes like 894 with lower

habitable structure counts.10

       Selecting a route with less habitable structures mitigates the risk of EMF exposure as

contemplated by the Commission’s rules, which is critical for the Walker Family. Due to the

proximity to the Walker Family’s homes, routes through Link J11, like Route 487, would fail to

conform to the policy of prudent avoidance.11 Mr. Walker expressed his concerns about the

potential effect of electromagnetic fields may have on his father’s pacemaker and reports that such

fields may cause cancer and other health issues.12 These concerns can and should be prudently

avoided through the adoption of Route 894 or any route not utilizing Link J11.

        2.         Route 894 parallels more than other alternative routes, including Route 487.

       Route 894 better tracks existing corridors than Route 487, limiting impacts to landowners.

The Commission’s routing rule, 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B), requires the consideration of

paralleling factors. This rule also encourages the line to be routed to reasonably moderate the

impact on the affected community and landowners. Paralleling existing corridors does just that.

       Similarly, 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B)(ii) compels consideration of whether routes parallel

existing public roads and highways. Route 894 is superior in this metric, paralleling existing roads

and highways for 4.45 miles, while Route 487 only does so for 3.75 miles.13

       In addition, 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B)(iii) requires the consideration of whether routes

parallel property lines or other natural or cultural features. Route 894 is superior on this metric as

well. Route 894 follows more property boundaries with 91.75 miles when compared to

Route 487’s 86.43 miles.14 Parallelling property boundaries is an important consideration for route

selection. Applicants’ witness, Mr. Marusak, testified that when developing routes, Applicants

always attempt to parallel to avoid bisecting and causing fragmentation of private property.15

       While Route 487 parallels a little over 10 more miles of existing right-of-way more than

894,16 this length fails to include transmission towers or similar infrastructure. This slight

difference makes no meaningful impact on landowners, leaving Route 894 superior given

comparison to the highlighted routing criteria above.

         3.         The length and cost differential between Routes 894 and 487 is negligible.

        The difference in length and cost between Route 894 and Route 487 is de minimis. Route

487 is less than two miles shorter than Route 894,17 a difference which does not tip the scales in

favor of 487. The Commission has no rule requiring the selection of the shortest route. The routing

criteria provides several factors which allow the Commission to moderate impacts on landowners,

and the shortest route is not always the least impactful. We see that here on a balanced review of

the factors.

        The projected cost difference is similarly negligible. Route 894 is “projected” to cost just

over $16 million more than Route 487.18 For a project where both Routes 894 and 487 will cost

over $1.5 billion, a difference of $16 million is not a material savings. Additionally, Applicants’

witness acknowledged that cost projections have no numerical margin of error, often change, and

are based on information and methodologies not readily verifiable at the time of filing.19

Applicants’ cost projections are merely conceptual and lack any site-specific design requirements;

requirements that can only be determined after a route is selected.20 Applicants’ witness,

Ms. Cooley, acknowledges that this lack of site-specific information may lead to a route that was

less expensive in the application becoming more expensive than other routes once installed.21 The

fact is, Applicants cannot truly rely on their cost projections until they have done site-specific

construction analysis of building costs.

 C.        Commission Staff’s Route 487 does not meet PURA’s statutory criteria and the
          Commission’s rules.

          The Commission Staff’s recommendation of Route 48722 is based on a flawed and

incomplete analysis performed by its engineer, John Poole. Mr. Poole testified that he attempts

“to read every filing in every proceeding in which [he is] giving a recommendation.”23 However,

Mr. Poole openly admits that he did not review all the filings in this proceeding before making a

recommendation.24             Specifically, before presenting his recommendation on behalf of the

Commission Staff, Mr. Poole failed to consider testimony and evidence relating to environmental

integrity (flood retarding structures), aesthetic values, historical values, prudent avoidance,

community values (schools), and recreational areas (Colorado Bend State Park). Accordingly, the

ALJs should reject the Commission Staff’s recommended route, Route 487, and any route that

includes Link J11.

          1.         Mr. Poole did not consider Route 487’s environmental impact on the Walker
                     Family’s property and on the flood retarding structure along Link J11.

          The ALJs should reject Route 487 because it fails to maintain the environmental integrity

along the Project and especially on Link J11.25 Sam Walker testified on behalf of the Walker

Family, explaining that he and his wife own an interest in the Brokenstar Ranch (the “Ranch”).26

Link J11, part of Route 487, crosses through the middle of the Ranch.27 Specifically, Link J11

crosses the main entry roadway of the Ranch and diagonally bisects the Walker’s Costal Bermuda

damage to trees, wildlife, and wildlife habitat that will be cleared for construction.29

        In addition, Link J11 crosses a flood retarding structure on the Ranch.30 The Lampasas

County Water Control & Improvement District #1 (“WCID”) manages and maintains flood

retarding structures in Lampasas County.31 The WCID’s Flood Retarding Structure #8 and its

structures are flood control dams, and the TCEQ has classified them as “High Hazard Dams.”33

Flood Retarding Structure #8 includes a large detention/retention pond.34

        Mr. Walker, a qualified civil-engineering expert,35 expressed his concerns about the impact

        route utilizing Link J11.36

These potential impacts are important considering that the City of Lampasas and the areas along

Sulphur Creek were prone to flooding, causing the loss of life and property, before WCID’s

       Mr. Walker also testified about several other environmental concerns with the routes

crossing Link J11. Mr. Walker described his concerns of potential impacts on groundwater below

the Ranch, which provides the only source of water for the family’s homes and livestock.39 He

also described concerns with geological and architectural features, such as cave and karst features,

geological formations, and pockets of silica and fossils.40

       Mr. Poole did not consider the environmental impact that Route 487 would have on the

Ranch and Flood Retarding Structure #8 when he made his recommendation.41 Mr. Poole admits

that the existence of flood retarding structures would have been relevant to his recommendation

and a fact he would have liked to know before making his recommendation.42 At the time of his

cross examination, Mr. Poole had read Mr. Walker’s direct testimony and had no reason to dispute

Mr. Walker’s concerns regarding the impacts a route through Link J11 would have on the flood

retarding structures.43 Mr. Poole, as well as the Applicants, also recognized that a route through

J11 would cross the southern portion of Flood Retarding Structure #8.44

project area. Route 894 crosses less linear miles of riparian areas (by approximately 8.89 miles),

        2.         Other PURA and Commission-rule factors, as applied to the Ranch, weigh
                   against adoption of Route 487.

        Several other relevant factors, such as aesthetic values, and historic values, make

Route 487 undesirable. To begin, any route that utilizes Link J11, such as Route 487, impairs

aesthetic values. As described above, Link J11 crosses through the middle of the Ranch and is

proposed to be between 500 to 1,000 feet north of both Mr. Walker’s home and his parents’ home.47

As PUC witness Mr. Poole testified, paralleling property reduces the negative aesthetic impacts

and fragmentations that would harm the Walkers by bisecting their land.48 Applicants’ witness,

Mr. Marusak, testified similarly, that paralleling is preferred because it creates less fragmentation

of land.49 The damage caused by construction of a route through Link J11 would wreck the natural

beauty that the Walker Family enjoys daily.50 In addition to being a massive eyesore, any route

crossing J11 would reduce the Ranch’s property value.51 On top of these concerns, a transmission

link through J11 will create a persistent humming or other noise, negatively impacting human and

wildlife in the area.52

          Finally, routes through Link J11 would also impact historical values. Mr. Walker testified

that there are known and unknown archaeological and Native American historical areas near and

adjacent to the Ranch that would be disrupted or destroyed by construction on the Link J11.53

Aesthetic values, prudent avoidance, and historical values caution against adopting any route

utilizing Link J11.

         3.          Route 487 is undesirable due to its proximity to Colorado Bend State Park,
                     implicating several PURA factors.

         The ALJs should not recommend adoption of any route utilizing Link J11, including

Route 487, because several PURA factors weigh heavily against doing so. Factors including

recreational and park areas, community values, and aesthetic values are all harmed by Link J11’s

extreme proximity to Colorado Bend State Park (“Colorado Bend”). Like the Ranch, Colorado

Bend is along Link J11.54 Specifically, Link J11 would cross the access road to Colorado Bend55

and run parallel to the park’s northern fenceline.56 The line’s proximity to the northern area of the

park would undoubtably create a massive eyesore. In fact, the centerline of any route utilizing

Link J11 would be 100 feet away from the edge of the Colorado Bend.57 Due to the proximity,

the route’s right-of-way would be cleared up to the edge of the park.58 Furthermore, use of Link

J11 would limit any future expansion of Colorado Bend. 59

can choose an alternative route if it wanted to avoid Colorado Bend.63 Applicants’ preferred route,

Route 894, does not utilize Link J11.

                                IV.      CONCLUSION AND PRAYER

       The record overwhelmingly supports a recommendation approving Route 894 and rejecting

Route 487. The record is clear that Route 894 is the route that best meets the overall requirements

of PURA § 37 and 16 TAC § 25.101. For these reasons, the Walker Family respectfully requests

that the ALJs issue a proposal for decision recommending Route 894.

     INTERVENOR THE WALKER FAMILY'S INITIAL POST-HEARING BRIEF

       Intervenors Sam Walker, John Walker, Jennifer Walker, and Lucy Walker (the "Walker

Family") file their Initial Post-Hearing Brief and request that the Administrative Law Judges

("ALJs") issue a proposal for decision recommending that the Public Utility Commission of Texas

(the "PUC" or "Commission") approve Applicants Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC

("Oncof') and LCRA Transmission Service Corporation ("LCRA")'s (collectively "Applicants")

recommended Route 894. In support of the requested relief, the Walker Family respectfully offers

the following:

                 I.   INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT

       Applicants seek approval from the Commission for the construction of a 765-kV

transmission line from Bell County south of Temple, Texas, to Big Hill, Texas, south of San

Angelo (the "Application" or the "Project"). Over the course ofthe five-day hearing on the merits,

Route 894, the Applicants' best meets route, proved to be just that, the best possible route that

should be approved by the Commission.




                                                3
        The evidence will show that Route 894 best satisfies Public Utility Regulatory Act' s

(" PURA' s") statutory factors on prudent avoidance, environmental integrity, paralleling, and

community values. None of the parties, including Commission Staff, put forth convincing

arguments for the Commission to disagree with the Applicants. In fact, Commission Staff would

have the Commission diverge from the best meets route, and select Route 487, despite admitting

his recommendation was made without reviewing the parties' testimonies. Any recommendation

with as significant of a record omission as this one cannot be relied upon by the Commission.

       Also critical, the Walker Family property on Link Jl 1 contains a large drainage facility,

the only flood retardant structure posed to be impacted by any route. As the record shows, the

Walker Family has reasonable environmental and safety concerns regarding the impacts of a

765-kV line crossing one of these structures. The record also shows that neither the Applicants nor

Commission Staff considered these impacts when selecting a line. Given the uncertainty of these

impacts, the prudent choice would be to avoid the drainage facilities all together. Selecting

Applicants Route 894 would do so.

       For the reasons explained below, the Walker Family respectfully requests that the ALJs

issue a Proposal for Decision selecting Route 894.

                                      III.    ARGUMENT

A.     Legal Standard

       An application for a certificate of convenience and necessity for a transmission line must

comply with the PIJRA. Specifically, Section 37.056 for "grant or denial of certificate" outlines

factors the Commission shall consider prior to approving an application. The Commission must

consider adequacy of existing service, community values, recreational and park areas, historical

and aesthetic values, and environmental integrity.2

       16 Texas Administrative Code ("TAC") § 25.101(b)(3)(B) requires that an application for

a new transmission line address the criteria set forth in PURA § 37.056(c) and, considering those

criteria, engineering constraints, and costs, the line must be routed to the extent reasonable to

moderate the impact on the affected community and landowners. Oncor and LCRA TSC' s

recommended Route 894 best meets the necessary criteria established by the Legislature for

approval of an application to amend Certificate of Convenience and Necessity ("CCN") while also

mitigating impacts to affected landowners. The criteria includes:

       (i)     whether the routes parallel or utilize existing compatible rights-of-way for
               electric facilities, including the use of vacant positions on existing multiple
               circuit transmission lines;

       (ii)    whether the routes parallel or utilize other existing compatible rights-of-
               way, including roads, highways, railroads, or telephone utility rights-of-
               vvay;

       (iii)   whether the routes parallel property lines or other natural or cultural
               features; and


       2 PURA § 37,056(c)(4)(A)-(E)

         (iv)     whether the routes conform with the policy of prudent avoidance.3

        The policy of prudent avoidance is a Commission routing principle intended to minimize

the exposure of the public to electric and magnetic fields ("EMF") and to avoid, where reasonable,

placing transmission facilities in close proximity to habitable structures and areas of concentrated

human activity.4 Routing moderation to avoid sensitive environmental features, whose degradation

could impact human activity, when there is little to no EMF exposure to the public is consistent

with the policy of prudent avoidance.

        2.      Route 894 parallels more than other alternative routes, including Route 487.

       Route 894 better tracks existing corridors than Route 487, limiting impacts to landowners.

The Commission's routing rule, 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B), requires the consideration of

paralleling factors. This rule also encourages the line to be routed to reasonably moderate the

impact on the affected community and landowners. Paralleling existing corridors does just that.

        Similarly, 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B)(ii) compels consideration of whether routes parallel

existing public roads and highways. Route 894 is superior in this metric, paralleling existing roads

and highways for 4.45 miles, while Route 487 only does so for 3.75 miles.13

       In addition, 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B)(iii) requires the consideration of whether routes

parallel property lines or other natural or cultural features. Route 894 is superior on this metric as

well. Route 894 follows more property boundaries with 91.75 miles when compared to

Route 487' s 86.43 miles.14 Parallelling property boundaries is an important consideration for route

selection. Applicants' witness, Mr. Marusak, testified that when developing routes, Applicants

always attempt to parallel to avoid bisecting and causing fragmentation of private property.15

       While Route 487 parallels a little over 10 more miles of existing right-of-way more than

894,16 this length fails to include transmission towers or similar infrastructure. This slight

difference makes no meaningful impact on landowners, leaving Route 894 superior given

comparison to the highlighted routing criteria above.

         3.       The length and cost differential between Routes 894 and 487 is negligible.

        The difference in length and cost between Route 894 and Route 487 is de minimis. Route

487 is less than two miles shorter than Route 894,17 a difference which does not tip the scales in

favor of 487. The Commission has no rule requiring the selection ofthe shortest route. The routing

criteria provides several factors which allow the Commission to moderate impacts on landowners,

and the shortest route is not always the least impactful. We see that here on a balanced review of

the factors.

        The projected cost difference is similarly negligible. Route 894 is "projected" to cost just

over $16 million more than Route 487.18 For a project where both Routes 894 and 487 will cost

over $1.5 billion, a difference of $16 million is not a material savings. Additionally, Applicants'

witness acknowledged that cost proj ections have no numerical margin of error, often change, and

are based on information and methodologies not readily verifiable at the time of filing. 19

Applicants' cost proj ections are merely conceptual and lack any site-specific design requirements;

requirements that can only be determined after a route is selected.20 Applicants' witness,

Ms. Cooley, acknowledges that this lack of site-specific information may lead to a route that was

less expensive in the application becoming more expensive than other routes once installed.21 The

fact is, Applicants cannot truly rely on their cost projections until they have done site-specific

construction analysis of building costs.
